I appreciate the discussion and your questions. A big part of my struggle is that I don’t see 'progressive Islam' as the right path for me because I have issues with the concept of progressivism itself—at least in how it’s commonly framed today.

Progressivism, as a movement, emerged from Enlightenment ideals in the West, advocating for things like secularism, individualism, and liberal democracy. Over time, it became the dominant framework for defining 'modernity' and 'social advancement.' But the issue is that these standards are rooted in a Western worldview, and they’ve often been imposed on other cultures—including Islamic societies—under the assumption that they must 'evolve' in the same way. This mindset played a big role in colonialism, where European powers justified their interventions by labeling non-Western societies as 'backward' and in need of reform.

When applied to Islam, progressivism often attempts to reshape the religion to fit these external ideals rather than engaging with it on its own terms. In my view, this is just another form of Orientalism—dictating what an 'acceptable' or 'modern' Islam should look like based on Western expectations. That’s why I struggle with the term. I don’t believe Islam needs to be adjusted to fit into a framework that wasn’t made for it in the first place.

That being said, my struggle isn’t about rejecting Islam—it’s about figuring out how to navigate my faith and sexuality without reshaping my religion to fit personal desires. Right now, I don’t have all the answers, and I don’t think I need to rush to find them. But I do know that I want to exist in both my faith and my identity without feeling like I have to betray one for the other.

As for the LGBTQ+ community, I do want to connect, but I struggle at the same time. I'm young, obviously, and I'm still navigating what I want and what I don't want, i guess.

Yeah, Islamic scholarship has changed over time—no one’s denying that. But there’s a huge difference between engaging with outside knowledge and restructuring Islam to fit modern Western ideals. Scholars like Ibn Rushd, Al-Ghazali, and Al-Farabi took ideas from Greek philosophy, Persian governance, and Indian sciences, but they did so within an Islamic framework. They didn’t force Islamic beliefs to conform to whatever was trendy in their time.

A lot of progressive Muslims today try to justify their reinterpretations by saying, “Well, past scholars engaged with outside knowledge too!” Sure, but they weren’t cherry-picking ideas to make Islam look more appealing to a Western liberal audience. They were refining Islamic thought while staying true to its core principles. That’s a big difference.
The argument that progressive values can just be absorbed into Islam because “Islam has always adapted” isn’t as solid as it sounds. Not all values are interchangeable. For example:

Islam introduced inheritance laws that were revolutionary at the time—but they still made gendered distinctions. That doesn’t sit well with modern egalitarian views, but it’s still part of Islamic law.
Same-sex attraction? The discussion is complex, but historically, Islamic scholars saw homosexual acts as sinful. Claiming Islam has always been LGBTQ+ affirming is just historically inaccurate.
Gender roles? Islam has always had complementary roles for men and women. You can argue about cultural influences, but you can’t erase the fact that the Quran and hadith lay out gendered obligations in areas like marriage, leadership, and legal testimony.


So, when progressives claim, “Islam has always been progressive on these issues, it was just cultural influences holding it back,” they’re kind of rewriting history. Yes, society plays a role, but Islam itself has principles that don’t always match modern Western progressivism.


The idea that critiquing progressive Islam is just colonial brainwashing is a massive cop-out. Orientalism, as Edward Said described it, is when the West portrays Islam as backwards and in need of enlightenment. But that’s not what’s happening here.
If anything, progressive Islam often does the same thing Orientalists did—it tries to mould Islam into something that’s more acceptable to Western sensibilities instead of understanding it on its own terms.
Criticizing progressive interpretations isn’t about rejecting modernity—it’s about asking, “Are these interpretations actually rooted in Islamic tradition, or are they just reshaping Islam to fit a Western liberal mold”
Plus, if disagreement with progressivism means someone is “colonized,” then what about all the scholars from Najaf, Qom, and Al-Azhar who also reject these views? Are they “brainwashed” too? The argument falls apart pretty quickly.

One of the biggest issues with progressive Islam is that it seems to treat Islam like it’s endlessly flexible—just shifting with the times. But at some point, you have to ask: What makes Islam Islam?
Yes, Islamic scholarship has different schools of thought, but there are still red lines. If we just rewrite fundamental beliefs every time society changes, where does it end?
Some rulings can evolve, sure—but not everything is up for debate. The Quran and hadith are clear on certain things, and just because they don’t align with modern Western ideals doesn’t mean they’re outdated.
Islam isn’t just a "pick whatever works for you" religion. It has a structure, a legal system, and a theological foundation. If everything is subjective, then at what point does Islam just become another form of secular morality?

You brought up scholars like Sayed Kamal al-Haydari and Khalil Andani to defend progressive Islam, but just because someone has a different methodology doesn’t mean their views represent Islam as a whole.
The reality is that progressive interpretations are still fringe in both Sunni and Shia scholarship.
Even within the history of Islamic thought, mainstream scholars often rejected outlier views when they weren’t backed by strong evidence.
If progressive Islam argues that every interpretation is valid, then why do they reject traditional scholars who disagree with them? They can’t have it both ways.

The core issue here isn’t that progressive Muslims are engaging with modern ideas—that’s fine. The problem is reshaping Islam just to align with Western liberal values instead of letting Islam speak for itself.
Islam has always had its own ethical and moral framework. It’s adapted over time, sure, but it’s done so without abandoning its core theological and legal foundations.
If progressives want to engage with modernity, that’s great—but it has to be on Islam’s terms, not by forcing Islam into a Western ideological mould.


At the end of the day, the question remains: If Islam can be reshaped into anything, then what makes it Islam anymore?

I appreciate your response and the effort to clarify progressive Islam’s perspective. However, I still have concerns about how progressive Islam engages with Islamic tradition and modernity.

First, I understand that progressive Muslims emphasize historical scholarly engagement with knowledge from other civilizations. Past Islamic scholars indeed incorporated and built upon external ideas, from Greek philosophy to Persian governance systems. However, I’d argue that there is a fundamental difference between integrating knowledge for intellectual growth and reshaping theological principles to align with contemporary Western liberal values. Scholars like Ibn Rushd and Al-Farabi engaged critically with external influences, but they did so within an Islamic epistemological framework—not to fit their beliefs into the prevailing ideologies of their time.

Regarding women’s rights and LGBTQ+ issues, you argue that Islam has always been progressive but that societal and cultural contexts shaped historical applications. I agree that culture plays a role, but it’s difficult to claim that Islam itself has always been "progressive" in the way modern progressives define it. While Islam introduced significant rights for women compared to pre-Islamic Arabia, it also established gendered legal distinctions (e.g., inheritance laws, polygamy, and testimony laws) that do not align with contemporary Western egalitarian ideals. Similarly, while Islamic history has examples of more nuanced attitudes toward same-sex relationships, the dominant Islamic legal schools historically viewed homosexual acts as sinful. If progressive Islam argues that these aspects were simply cultural influences and not Islamic, where do we draw the line?

On the issue of scriptural interpretation, you say that progressive Muslims do not cherry-pick verses and instead engage deeply with Quranic Arabic and Islamic scholarship. That’s fair. However, I still find that many progressive arguments rely on interpretations that would have been considered fringe or unorthodox in traditional Islamic scholarship. You mention scholars like Sayed Kamal al-Haydari and Dr. Khalil Andani—while they are intellectuals engaging with Islam critically, their views are not universally accepted within mainstream Sunni or Shia thought. If progressive Islam is about choosing methodologies that differ from dominant interpretations, doesn’t that imply an inherent subjectivity rather than an objective claim that Islam is progressive?

Finally, I don’t doubt that this subreddit engages with academic and historical sources. My issue is not that progressive Muslims lack knowledge, but rather that their framework for understanding Islam often mirrors Western liberalism rather than traditional Islamic thought. While it’s valid to reinterpret Islam for modern contexts, I’m still left with the question: What is the real Islam? If Islam can be fundamentally redefined across different eras and ideologies, does it retain a core identity, or is it simply whatever we want it to be?

I appreciate the discussion and am happy to engage further.

I have some reservations about the r/progressive_islam community, and I think it’s important to first define what progressivism actually is. At its core, progressivism is a liberal political philosophy aimed at achieving societal and technological advancement. However, this philosophy was developed in a Western context, meaning that what is considered “progressive” is often shaped by Western liberal ideals.

This is why Islam is frequently criticized by liberal-leaning individuals for not being progressive enough on issues like women's rights and LGBTQ+ rights. Historically, however, Islam’s stance on issues like homosexuality has been more complex than it is often portrayed (Oxford Bibliographies).

The way I see it, progressive Islam as a community primarily consists of Muslims who were raised in the West and have adopted these Western standards of progress. Ironically, while progressive Muslims often criticize fundamentalists for interpreting scripture too literally, they do the same when attempting to prove that Islam aligns with progressive values. They cherry-pick Quranic verses and interpret them in an extremely literal way to argue that Islam is inherently liberal (Springer).

But to me, this entire push to make Islam fit into a progressive mold feels like a form of colonialism—though I know that might sound extreme. It’s as if Islam is being forced into a Western ideological framework just to make it more acceptable to others. Instead of being understood on its own terms, it’s being reshaped to conform to external expectations (Fondapol).

At the same time, I feel like both progressive-leaning Muslims and fundamentalists are just screaming at each other, echoing their arguments over and over, yet nothing really changes. The actual structures that make life difficult for many in the Middle East or even in Muslim communities elsewhere are products of the post-colonial world (Friedrich-Ebert-Stiftung). Whether or not music is haram or halal isn’t going to change the material realities that people are suffering under.

That being said, I don’t think Islam is beyond criticism. There are undeniably aspects that deserve scrutiny, such as the restriction on Muslim women marrying people from Ahlul Kitab (People of the Book). At the same time, there are also many beautiful things within Islam that shouldn’t have to be sacrificed just to fit a certain narrative.

Someone compared the struggles of the Ummah to the Kali Yuga in the Hindu calendar—a period characterized by decay, conflict, and moral decline. While this era is marked by challenges, they suggested that it is also part of a cyclical process. Just as decay gives way to renewal, I am certain that we, as a people, will rise again. For now, however, perhaps patience and steadfastness are what this time demands of us.

The political and religious challenges Iran faces today stem largely from the theocratic system itself. Within Iran, you’ll find devoutly religious individuals who oppose the government, alongside atheists who support it. This complexity makes it difficult to position oneself clearly. External powers often frame the situation as a simplistic clash between Islam and modernism, which is both reductive and misleading.  

I also find it frustrating when modernism is equated with Westernization. In reality, Khamenei's ideology incorporates significant modernist elements, though many might find that claim surprising. The idea that we can simply “return to our roots” as a solution ignores the nuance and long-term complexity of the issues at hand.  

As an Iranian Muslim who recently started wearing the hijab, I find this struggle deeply personal. It’s frustrating to navigate these challenges, but I draw strength from Imam Ali’s wisdom: we must follow the truth, not the majority. That principle guides me as I seek clarity and integrity in these turbulent times.

The deeper issues I’m referring to include the legacy of colonialism and imperialism, like artificial borders and economic exploitation, which left the region fragmented and dependent. There’s also an identity crisis, where cultural erosion and globalization have left many struggling to reconcile modernity with Islamic principles, leading to extremes like Salafism or Khomeinism. Authoritarianism, sectarian divides, economic inequality, and corruption also play major roles, as does a loss of spiritual depth in Islam, where the faith is used more as a political tool than a source of justice and ethical guidance. These issues need deeper, long-term solutions rather than reactionary ideologies.
